vectors.name: if-evaluates-exactly-one-branch
vectors.note: The untaken branch is not evaluated: a division by zero there is never reached.

vectors.name: let-is-sequential
vectors.note: let* semantics: each binding sees the earlier ones.

vectors.name: let-rebinding-in-one-list-is-permitted
vectors.note: Ordinary let*: the second binding's expression sees the first's value.

vectors.name: let-binding-is-not-recursive
vectors.note: A binding's expression cannot reference its own name. Rejected; the code is diagnostic (§10).

vectors.name: let-shadowing-true-is-a-parse-error
vectors.note: true/false/null are literals in the grammar (§3.1), not symbols, so this fails at parse -- a different code from shadowing a special form, which §10 rejects.

vectors.name: and-returns-the-first-falsy-value
vectors.note: Not a bool: and returns the offending *value*, which is what makes (and $a $b) usable as a value expression.

vectors.name: fn-closes-over-its-environment
vectors.note: Lexical closure over the enclosing environment.

vectors.name: fn-parameters-bind-simultaneously
vectors.note: The argument `a` is the outer binding, not the parameter being bound: parameters bind simultaneously, unlike let.

vectors.name: builtin-name-is-a-function-value
vectors.note: A symbol resolving to the builtin table yields a function, which is what makes this legal. There is no second kind of callable.

vectors.name: function-bound-by-let-then-applied
vectors.note: Functions flow as operands -- bound by let, passed to a builtin, applied directly -- but never into a value.

vectors.name: function-cannot-enter-a-collection
vectors.note: Functions are not CBOR values, so they cannot be stored in a collection.

vectors.name: recursion-is-unconstructible
vectors.note: A function cannot name itself: no define, no letrec, no self-reference. This is what makes termination structural rather than fuel-dependent.

vectors.name: applying-a-non-function
vectors.note: The head is a list, so what it evaluates to is not statically decidable and 10 leaves this to evaluation -- which is what makes TYPE normative here. The decidable heads, (1 2) and ($temp 1), are rejected at configure time instead and live in analysis.json, where 10 makes the code diagnostic rather than normative.
